questions.question: An administrator needs to insert a FortiGate into an existing network between two switches without changing IP addressing on any device. The FortiGate should pass all traffic transparently and apply security policies. Which deployment mode achieves this?
options: Transparent mode, where the FortiGate acts as a Layer-2 bridge with no IP address on physical interfaces
Sniffer (one-armed) mode tapping a SPAN port, with IPS sensors providing passive detection only
NAT/Route mode with policy-based routing rules that preserve original source addresses end-to-end
Virtual-wire pair binding two interfaces together so that traffic is forwarded only between that pair
questions.explanation: Transparent mode turns the FortiGate into a Layer-2 bridge: physical interfaces carry no IP, traffic flows through unchanged, and security policies still apply — exactly the requirement. Sniffer mode is passive and cannot block, so policies have no enforcement path. NAT/Route mode requires IP addresses on every interface, breaking the 'no addressing change' constraint. Virtual-wire pair is inline like transparent mode but binds the two ports rigidly together; it is used for tap-style inspection between a fixed pair, not as a general L2 firewall sitting between two switches that may need to learn many MACs.

questions.question: A security analyst notices that a FortiGate security policy is matching traffic but the actions from the attached IPS profile are not taking effect. What is the most likely cause?
options: The FortiGuard IPS signature database has not been updated recently, so the older signatures no longer match modern traffic patterns
The policy uses flow-based inspection, and IPS profiles only run in proxy-based inspection mode in typical FortiOS deployments
The IPS profile is in monitor mode, so matches are logged but never blocked for the workloads described in the scenario under the standard FortiGate configuration
The FortiGate is running in NGFW (policy-based) mode, where IPS is enabled directly on the policy and the legacy 'profile' attachment is ignored
questions.explanation: FortiOS supports two inspection architectures: profile-based (legacy — security profiles are attached to a policy) and NGFW / policy-based (security capabilities are configured directly on the policy). When the FortiGate is switched to NGFW mode, the legacy IPS profile attachment is no longer consulted, so its actions appear to do nothing — IPS must be enabled at the policy level instead. Old signatures (A) would mean missed matches, not matches with no action. IPS works fine in both flow and proxy modes, so (B) is wrong. Monitor-mode (C) would still produce visible IPS log entries with action=detected; here the issue is that the profile is not consulted at all.

questions.question: FortiGuard provides various subscription services. An administrator wants to enable URL category-based web filtering on a FortiGate. Which FortiGuard subscription must be active?
options: FortiGuard Application Control subscription, which identifies applications by protocol behavior
FortiGuard IPS subscription, which provides signature-based threat detection in typical FortiOS deployments
FortiGuard AntiVirus subscription, which scans downloaded files for malware for the workloads described in the scenario
FortiGuard Web Filtering subscription, which provides URL category ratings from Fortinet's global database
questions.explanation: URL category-based filtering relies on the FortiGuard Web Filtering service: Fortinet maintains a cloud database that classifies hundreds of millions of URLs into categories (social media, gambling, malware, etc.) and FortiGate queries it to decide allow/block. Application Control identifies traffic by protocol and behavior, not by URL category. IPS detects exploits and intrusion patterns, not URL categories. AntiVirus inspects file content. None of those three subscriptions provides URL category ratings.

questions.question: An administrator must prevent all users on the internal network from accessing social media sites during business hours (08:00–17:00, Mon–Fri) but allow access outside these hours. What combination of FortiGate features achieves this?
options: Two security policies referencing a web filter profile that blocks social media categories, with a recurring schedule (Mon–Fri 08:00–17:00) on the blocking policy
IP-based ACLs sourced from FortiGuard IP reputation feeds, blocking known social media IP ranges in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
An application control profile blocking social media categories, attached to a single 24×7 security policy under the standard FortiGate configuration
A DNS filter profile blocking social media categories with time-based exceptions configured in the DNS policy when applied at the security-policy level
questions.explanation: Time-based access on FortiGate is implemented by binding a schedule object to a security policy. The classic pattern is two policies evaluated top-down: the upper policy uses the Mon–Fri 08:00–17:00 schedule plus a web filter profile that blocks social media; the lower policy has no schedule and a permissive profile. Outside business hours the upper policy does not match and the lower one allows traffic. IP-feed ACLs (B) cannot cover modern CDN-hosted social media accurately. A single 24×7 application control policy (C) blocks all the time, ignoring the time requirement. DNS filter (D) cannot apply time-based exceptions per query in this granular way.

questions.question: A FortiGate has two WAN interfaces: WAN1 (100 Mbps, primary ISP) and WAN2 (50 Mbps, backup ISP). The administrator wants traffic to use WAN1 unless it goes down, then automatically fail over to WAN2. What FortiGate feature achieves this?
options: Policy-based routing rules that match all internal traffic and forward it out WAN1, with WAN2 as a static fallback in the route map
Two equal-priority default static routes (one per WAN) and ECMP load-balancing across both interfaces
BGP peering on both WAN interfaces, advertising the internal prefix to both ISPs with AS-path prepending for the secondary
An SD-WAN zone with WAN1 and WAN2 as members and a performance SLA that triggers failover when WAN1's health check fails
questions.explanation: FortiGate's SD-WAN feature is the recommended way to handle multi-WAN failover: define both WAN interfaces as SD-WAN members, attach a performance SLA (ping/HTTP probe to a known target) and set the rule to prefer WAN1; when the SLA fails, traffic is automatically steered to WAN2. Policy-based routing (A) does not include built-in liveness probing of the primary. Equal-priority static routes with ECMP (B) would load-balance — the customer wants strict primary/standby. BGP (C) requires ISP cooperation and is far heavier than necessary for a two-link active/standby scenario.

questions.question: An administrator needs to allow external users on the internet to access an internal web server (192.168.1.100) on port 80 via the FortiGate's WAN IP (203.0.113.10). Which FortiGate NAT feature should be configured?
options: A Central SNAT entry mapping the internal server to the WAN interface for outbound replies in typical FortiOS deployments
A policy-based DNAT object that rewrites the destination address inside the policy match conditions for the workloads described in the scenario
A Virtual IP (VIP) with external IP 203.0.113.10 and mapped IP 192.168.1.100, referenced as the destination in a WAN-to-LAN policy
An IP Pool of type overload binding 203.0.113.10 to the LAN subnet so external traffic is reflected back under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: Inbound port forwarding on FortiGate is configured as a Virtual IP (VIP), which performs destination NAT (DNAT): external IP = the public address users hit, mapped IP = the internal server. A WAN-to-LAN security policy then references the VIP as its destination. Central SNAT (A) only translates source addresses on outbound flows, so it cannot accept inbound connections. FortiGate has no standalone 'policy-based DNAT' object separate from VIPs (B). IP Pools (D) are used for SNAT translation and overload, not for inbound destination NAT.

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator wants to ensure that outgoing traffic from the LAN network (192.168.1.0/24) appears to come from the FortiGate's WAN IP address (203.0.113.10) when leaving the network. What NAT configuration achieves this?
options: Enable NAT on the LAN-to-WAN security policy so the FortiGate translates source addresses to the outgoing interface IP
Configure a Virtual IP with the LAN subnet as the mapped range and the WAN IP as the external address
Configure DNAT on the WAN interface with the LAN subnet as the original destination in typical FortiOS deployments
Disable stateful inspection on the LAN-to-WAN policy and rely on the global gateway for SNAT for the workloads described in the scenario
questions.explanation: The simplest and most common way to source-NAT outbound LAN traffic to the WAN IP is to enable NAT on the security policy: FortiGate then rewrites the source address to the outgoing interface's IP (using port translation for many-to-one). A Virtual IP (B) is for inbound destination NAT, not for translating outbound source traffic. DNAT (C) translates destinations, not sources. Disabling stateful inspection (D) does not perform NAT at all — it would break the firewall function entirely. (Central SNAT is also a valid alternative but is not offered here; enabling NAT on the policy is the direct answer.)

questions.question: A FortiGate IPS profile is set to Block for a known exploit signature. During testing, the FortiGate logs the IPS match but does not block the traffic. What should the administrator verify first?
options: That the FortiGuard IPS subscription is still active so new pattern files keep arriving in typical FortiOS deployments
That the SSL/SSH inspection profile on the policy is in 'deep-inspection' mode and covers the relevant port for the workloads described in the scenario
That the IPS sensor's filter (category/severity/OS) entries do not override the individual signature action with 'Monitor' or 'Pass'
That the policy uses proxy-based inspection mode instead of flow-based under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: Inside an IPS sensor, both filter entries (matching by category/severity/OS) and individual signature entries can set actions. If a higher-priority filter entry covering that category is set to 'Monitor' or 'Pass', it overrides the per-signature 'Block' — IPS logs the match but doesn't enforce the action. That is the most common cause of 'logged but not blocked'. The subscription being expired (A) would stop new signatures, not change how existing ones act. SSL deep inspection (B) is needed for HTTPS-borne exploits but does not by itself silence the block. IPS runs in both flow and proxy mode (D), so the inspection mode is not the root cause here.

questions.question: An administrator must ensure a FortiGate high-availability (HA) active-passive cluster maintains session continuity so that existing TCP sessions are not dropped during a failover. Which HA feature must be enabled?
options: Heartbeat interface monitoring so the secondary detects a primary failure quickly in typical FortiOS deployments
Gratuitous ARP on the cluster's interfaces so neighboring switches relearn the new MAC quickly after a failover
Session pickup (session synchronization), which mirrors the active session table from primary to secondary
Virtual MAC addressing on cluster interfaces so the failover is transparent to the L2 fabric
questions.explanation: Session pickup (sometimes called session synchronization) is the HA feature that continuously replicates the primary's session table to the secondary; on failover the secondary already knows about each in-flight TCP flow and can forward it without resetting the connection. Heartbeat (A) detects that a failure occurred but doesn't replicate state. Gratuitous ARP (B) and virtual MAC (D) handle the L2 cutover so packets reach the new active unit, but neither preserves session state — without session pickup the secondary still drops existing TCP flows.

questions.question: A company deploys FortiGate in active-active HA mode. The administrator notices that the secondary unit is not processing any traffic despite being healthy. What is the most likely cause?
options: Active-active mode only activates the secondary if the primary fails, so this is expected behavior in typical FortiOS deployments
The HA load-balancing schedule is not configured (or is set to 'none'), so the primary keeps all sessions instead of distributing them
Active-active mode requires a separate FortiGate license on the secondary unit to process traffic for the workloads described in the scenario
The secondary's interfaces must be plugged into a different switch than the primary for load distribution to work under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: In active-active HA the primary unit receives all traffic and distributes new sessions to cluster members based on the configured HA load-balancing schedule (by source IP, by source-dest IP, etc.). If the schedule is 'none' or unconfigured the primary processes everything itself, leaving the secondary idle even though it is healthy. (A) describes active-passive, not active-active. There is no separate per-unit license requirement (C). HA does not require dual-switch attachment (D) — that is a redundancy concern, not a load-balancing one.

questions.question: A FortiGate SSL inspection profile is configured for 'deep inspection' but users report certificate errors when accessing HTTPS banking sites. The administrator wants to exempt banking sites from SSL inspection. What should be configured?
options: A custom application signature for each bank, then excluded from the SSL profile via Application Control in typical FortiOS deployments
An exemption list inside the SSL/SSH inspection profile, using either specific addresses or the 'Finance and Banking' URL category
A separate security policy for banking traffic with SSL inspection disabled and placed above the general policy
Add the FortiGate CA certificate to the bank-site issuer block list to skip re-signing for the workloads described in the scenario
questions.explanation: SSL/SSH inspection profiles contain a built-in 'Exempt from SSL Inspection' list keyed on addresses, FortiGuard URL categories, or specific web ratings — adding banking sites (or the 'Finance and Banking' category) bypasses interception for them, avoiding the certificate-pinning errors. Custom application signatures (A) identify protocols but do not feed into the SSL exemption list. A separate policy without SSL inspection (C) does work in principle but is harder to maintain than the built-in exemption list. Adding the FortiGate CA to a 'block' list (D) would not exempt anything; it would break the trust chain in the opposite direction.

questions.question: An administrator needs to authenticate users on the internal network using their Active Directory credentials when they access the internet through FortiGate, without requiring users to enter credentials manually. Which FortiGate feature achieves transparent AD authentication?
options: LDAP authentication with FortiGate polling AD for group membership every 30 seconds in typical FortiOS deployments
Fortinet Single Sign-On (FSSO) using the DC Agent or Collector Agent to read Windows logon events and map users to IPs
RADIUS authentication with AD as the backend and a captive portal for sign-in for the workloads described in the scenario
FortiAuthenticator 802.1X with EAP-TLS at the access switches under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: FSSO is Fortinet's transparent SSO mechanism: a DC Agent on each domain controller (or a Collector Agent polling DC event logs) reads Windows logon events (event ID 4624), builds a user-to-IP mapping, and pushes it to the FortiGate, which can then enforce identity-based policies with no user prompt. Plain LDAP (A) authenticates a user on each connection — it is not transparent. RADIUS with captive portal (C) prompts every user. 802.1X (D) is a network-access mechanism at the switch and does not by itself give FortiGate the user-to-IP mapping needed for identity-aware policies.

questions.question: An administrator creates a new admin account on FortiGate with the 'Read Only' profile. The new admin reports they cannot run diagnose commands in the CLI. What is the reason?
options: The FortiGate prompts for a separate administrator password before running any diagnose command in typical FortiOS deployments
Diagnose commands require a Fortinet support account to be linked to the administrator profile for the workloads described in the scenario
The built-in Read-Only profile permits get/show but not the diagnostic command tree; a custom profile or super_admin is needed
Read-Only admins must be assigned an additional SSH access profile to use the CLI at all under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: FortiGate admin profiles control which command trees an administrator can use. The built-in Read-Only profile allows 'get' and 'show' (view configuration) but does not include access to the 'diagnose' tree, which is treated as a higher privilege. To allow it, either elevate the admin to super_admin or create a custom profile that explicitly grants the system/network diagnostics permissions. There is no second-password prompt for diagnose (A). Fortinet support accounts (B) are unrelated to admin RBAC. There is no separate 'SSH access profile' construct (D) — CLI access is governed by the admin profile and trusted hosts.

questions.question: A FortiGate is configured with multiple security policies. Traffic from the LAN is being denied despite a policy that should allow it. What is the most likely reason?
options: The implicit deny at the bottom of the policy list runs first by default and blocks the traffic
The source address object in the allow policy is FQDN-based and DNS resolution is failing
FortiGate's default action on every policy is Deny, even when the administrator selected Accept
A higher-priority policy further up the list matches the traffic first and denies it
questions.explanation: FortiGate evaluates security policies top-down and uses the first match — once a policy matches, no further policies are consulted. If a deny policy (or a more specific allow policy with logging-only) appears above the intended allow policy, it claims the traffic and blocks it; the implicit deny at the bottom is only reached when nothing matched. (A) inverts the actual order — the implicit deny is last, not first. FQDN resolution failure (B) is rare and would produce empty address sets, not a generic 'denied' result. (C) is simply not how FortiGate behaves: the configured Accept action takes effect.

questions.question: An administrator wants to prevent internal users from using applications like BitTorrent and Tor regardless of port or protocol. Which FortiGate security profile should be used?
options: An IPS profile with BitTorrent and Tor signatures set to Block in typical FortiOS deployments
A Web Filter profile with the Peer-to-Peer and Proxy categories set to Block
A DNS Filter profile blocking known BitTorrent tracker and Tor relay domains
An Application Control profile with the BitTorrent and Tor / Anonymizer categories set to Block
questions.explanation: Application Control performs deep packet inspection and behavioral fingerprinting, so it identifies applications even when they hop ports or wrap themselves in TLS — exactly what BitTorrent and Tor do. IPS (A) targets exploits, not application use. Web Filter (B) categorizes URLs and cannot identify a protocol that doesn't talk HTTP. DNS Filter (C) only catches the lookup step, and Tor and modern BitTorrent clients use bootstrap lists / DHT that often bypass plain DNS queries.

questions.question: FortiGate is configured with an active-passive HA cluster. After a power failure on the primary, the secondary unit takes over. When the primary comes back online, what happens by default?
options: The primary unit immediately reclaims the active role and demotes the current active unit in typical FortiOS deployments
The secondary keeps the active role; the recovered primary becomes the new standby until a manual failover is performed
Both units enter renegotiation and the higher serial number wins for the workloads described in the scenario
Both units go into a degraded state until firmware versions are re-validated under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: By default, FortiGate HA runs without 'override' enabled. That means there is no preemption: once the secondary becomes active, it stays active even after the original primary returns to health — the returning unit becomes the standby. This minimizes disruption (no second failover when the primary recovers). With override enabled, the unit with the higher priority can preempt. (A) describes override-enabled behavior, which is not the default. (C) and (D) are not how FortiGate HA arbitrates.

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator needs to enable remote management access via HTTPS only on the WAN interface for a specific administrator's IP address (198.51.100.5). What two configurations are required?
options: Allow HTTPS through a WAN-to-FortiGate firewall policy with source 198.51.100.5 and service HTTPS in typical FortiOS deployments
Enable HTTPS on the WAN interface and reference the address object 198.51.100.5 in the admin profile
Enable HTTPS administrative access on the WAN interface and set trusted hosts on the admin account to 198.51.100.5/32
Place the WAN interface in an admin-only security zone and rely on the zone for source filtering for the workloads described in the scenario
questions.explanation: Two pieces are required: (1) the WAN interface must list HTTPS among its allowed administrative-access protocols, and (2) the admin account's 'trusted hosts' field must scope which source IPs may log in to that account — set it to 198.51.100.5/32. Regular firewall policies (A) govern transit traffic, not management traffic destined for the FortiGate itself (that's controlled by per-interface administrative access plus local-in policies). Admin profiles (B) control permissions, not source-IP scoping. Security zones (D) do not have built-in admin source filtering.

questions.question: A user reports they cannot access a specific website. The FortiGate web filter log shows the site is blocked under the 'Unrated' category. The administrator verifies the site is legitimate. What is the quickest solution?
options: Add the site's URL to a Web Filter URL override list with action Allow so it is whitelisted immediately
Disable Unrated-category blocking globally so any unclassified URL is allowed in typical FortiOS deployments
Submit the site to FortiGuard for re-categorization and wait for the global rating database to update
Reboot the FortiGate so the local rating cache is rebuilt from FortiGuard for the workloads described in the scenario
questions.explanation: URL overrides inside a web filter profile take precedence over category-based rules and apply instantly — adding the URL with action Allow unblocks the user immediately. Disabling Unrated globally (B) is a heavy-handed security regression. Submitting for re-categorization (C) is the right long-term fix but can take days. Rebooting (D) does nothing to change the rating, only refreshing it from the same FortiGuard source.

questions.question: An administrator needs to configure a site-to-site IPsec VPN between a FortiGate (HQ) and a branch office FortiGate. Both have static public IPs. The tunnel must use IKEv2 with pre-shared key authentication. Which Phase 1 settings are mandatory?
options: Remote gateway IP, the Phase 2 subnet selectors, and the IKEv2 fragmentation MTU value
Remote gateway IP, pre-shared key, IKE version set to 2, plus encryption and authentication proposals
ISAKMP port (UDP 500), remote gateway IP, and NAT-Traversal enabled in all cases in typical FortiOS deployments
Remote gateway IP, an X.509 certificate, and a DH group, since IKEv2 requires certificate authentication
questions.explanation: Phase 1 (the IKE SA) negotiates the secure channel that will then carry Phase 2. Its mandatory inputs are: the remote peer address, the authentication credential (here a pre-shared key), the IKE version (set to 2 for IKEv2), and the proposals for encryption / integrity / DH group. Phase 2 selectors (A) belong to Phase 2, not Phase 1. UDP 500 is the standard ISAKMP port but NAT-T is not always required (C) — only when one end is behind NAT. IKEv2 does not require certificates (D); PSK and certificate authentication are both valid.

questions.question: Remote workers need to access internal company resources using FortiGate SSL VPN. After connecting via the web portal, users can only access the resources listed in the portal bookmarks, not arbitrary internal IPs. What must be configured to allow full network access?
options: Buy an upgrade license that converts the SSL VPN portal from web-only to full tunnel mode in typical FortiOS deployments
Enable split tunneling in the SSL VPN profile so that all traffic is routed through the FortiGate for the workloads described in the scenario
Re-add each internal subnet as a bookmark in the web portal under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
Enable Tunnel Mode in the SSL VPN portal and assign an IP pool so FortiClient gets a virtual adapter with routed LAN access
questions.explanation: SSL VPN operates in two modes: Web Mode is a clientless browser portal that can only reach the bookmarks you configure, while Tunnel Mode requires FortiClient and presents a virtual NIC to the operating system, giving access to any internal IP allowed by routing and policy. Enabling Tunnel Mode and configuring an IP pool is the standard solution. There is no special 'full tunnel license' (A) — Tunnel Mode is part of the base SSL VPN feature. Split tunneling (B) governs which traffic goes through the tunnel once Tunnel Mode is up; it does not turn Tunnel Mode on. Bookmarks (C) only address curated apps, not arbitrary IPs.

questions.question: An administrator wants FortiGate to inspect encrypted HTTPS traffic for malware. Users are reporting browser warnings about untrusted certificates on all HTTPS sites. What is the correct resolution?
options: Switch the inspection mode to certificate-inspection only so no re-signing happens in typical FortiOS deployments
Export the FortiGate's built-in CA certificate and install it as a trusted root in client browsers (e.g. via Group Policy or MDM)
Buy a publicly-trusted wildcard certificate (*.example.com) and install it on the FortiGate as its CA for the workloads described in the scenario
Enable a certificate-transparency bypass option so browsers do not validate the substituted certificate under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: When FortiGate performs deep SSL inspection it acts as a TLS man-in-the-middle: it re-signs each server certificate with its own CA. Browsers reject that signature unless they already trust the FortiGate CA. The fix is to deploy the FortiGate CA cert as a trusted root on every client (Group Policy, MDM, etc.) so the re-signed certs validate cleanly. Certificate inspection (A) avoids the warning but also removes the ability to inspect payload — which contradicts the requirement. Public wildcard certs (C) cannot be used as a CA — a public CA will never issue you a signing CA cert. There is no 'certificate-transparency bypass' switch in browsers (D).

questions.question: FortiOS antivirus scanning can operate in two inspection modes. A large enterprise needs to scan files up to 500MB. Which inspection mode supports scanning large files and how does it work?
options: Flow-based inspection, because it streams without buffering and therefore has no file-size limit
Proxy-based inspection, because it buffers the entire file before delivery and supports large files plus heuristics
Flow-based inspection, because it buffers the file in chunks and can scan files of any size in typical FortiOS deployments
Either mode — the file-size cap is purely a license setting and is not influenced by inspection mode
questions.explanation: Proxy-based inspection terminates the protocol at the FortiGate, buffers the complete file, scans it (signatures + heuristics + content-disarm), then delivers it. That buffering is what lets it handle large files up to the configured 'oversize file' limit. Flow-based inspection examines packets as they pass and intentionally does not buffer entire files (A/B) — it can miss content that crosses packet boundaries and has stricter size limits. Licensing (D) determines whether AV is available, not whether large files are scannable.

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator needs to run diagnostic commands on FortiGate to capture network packets traversing through the firewall. Which CLI command initiates a packet capture?
options: debug packet capture interface <name> filter <expression> count <n>
diagnose debug flow filter add interface <name>
diagnose sniffer packet <interface> '<filter>' <verbosity> <count>
show interfaces capture filter <expression> detail
questions.explanation: The FortiOS packet-capture utility is `diagnose sniffer packet <interface> '<filter>' <verbosity> <count>`. The filter uses BPF/tcpdump syntax, verbosity ranges from 1 (headers only) up to 6 (with hex + interface details), and count limits how many packets to capture. The other commands do not exist as written: there is no `debug packet capture` command (A); `diagnose debug flow filter add` is part of the flow-trace tool, not packet capture (B); and `show interfaces capture` is not a valid CLI (D).

questions.question: A FortiGate is configured to use RADIUS for admin authentication. An administrator logs in successfully but gets 'permission denied' when trying to access certain configuration areas. What is the likely cause?
options: The RADIUS server is accepting the user but the matching admin account on the FortiGate has a restrictive (e.g. Read-Only) profile that takes effect when no Fortinet VSA returns a different one

RADIUS authentication on FortiGate cannot carry profile information; only locally-defined admin accounts can have admin profiles in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario

The RADIUS timeout is too low and the Fortinet-Group-Name VSA arrives after the session begins, defaulting to no permissions under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level

The administrator is a member of multiple RADIUS groups and FortiGate intersects their permissions, leaving them with no rights in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
questions.explanation: FortiGate maps a RADIUS-authenticated admin to an admin profile in two ways: by reading the Fortinet-Group-Name VSA returned by RADIUS, or — if no VSA is returned — by the profile defined on the matching wildcard / RADIUS-backed admin account. If that local account's profile is restrictive (Read-Only or a custom subset), the admin logs in but lacks permissions. Statement (B) is false: RADIUS admins absolutely can have profiles assigned. There is no race condition like (C). FortiGate uses the first matched profile, not a permission intersection (D).

questions.question: A FortiGate security policy uses proxy-based inspection with a web filter profile. An administrator notices that some web traffic bypasses the web filter checks. After investigation, they find the traffic uses HTTPS on port 8443. What is the most likely cause?
options: Web filter cannot operate on TCP ports above 1024; only well-known port ranges are inspectable in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Port 8443 requires a custom Application Control signature before any web filter can be applied under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level

Proxy-based mode only inspects HTTPS when the FortiGate is the explicit proxy; transparent deployments cannot inspect non-443 HTTPS in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
The policy's service object covers only standard HTTPS (443), so traffic to port 8443 doesn't match; a service covering 8443 is needed (and the SSL inspection profile must include 8443 too)
questions.explanation: A FortiGate security policy matches on its service object. The default HTTPS service is TCP/443 only — traffic on 8443 falls through to a different (probably permissive) policy or simply isn't matched by the web-filtered policy at all. Adding a service for TCP/8443 (or using ALL) and including 8443 in the SSL inspection profile's port list lets the proxy decrypt and filter that traffic. There is no 'no inspection above port 1024' rule (A). Web filter does not require an Application Control signature first (B). Proxy-based inspection works in both transparent and explicit modes (C).

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator needs to verify whether a specific IP address matches any firewall policy and which policy it would match. Which diagnostic tool is most effective for this?
options: Manually filter the traffic log by source IP after asking the user to retry, then read the matched policy ID from the log entry in typical FortiOS deployments
Use Policy Lookup in the GUI (Policy & Objects > Policy Lookup) with the source/destination/service to see which policy would match without generating live traffic
Run `diagnose debug flow trace start` and ask the user to reproduce live traffic for the flow trace for the workloads described in the scenario under the standard FortiGate configuration
Open Forward Traffic logs and sort by hit count to infer policy matching for the given IP when applied at the security-policy level in a single-VDOM topology
questions.explanation: Policy Lookup is purpose-built for this question: enter source, destination, protocol, port (and optionally interface), and FortiGate returns the policy that would be selected, without needing real traffic. Reading traffic logs (A) only works if traffic actually flowed and was logged. `diagnose debug flow` (C) traces live packets — useful for deep troubleshooting but heavier than a static lookup. Sorting Forward Traffic logs by hit count (D) doesn't tell you which policy a given IP would match; it just shows aggregate counters.

questions.question: FortiGate is running in profile-based inspection mode. An administrator wants to inspect file downloads for malware in both HTTP and FTP traffic using the same antivirus profile. How should the profile be applied?
options: Build two antivirus profiles (one per protocol) and attach each to a separate protocol-specific policy in typical FortiOS deployments
Antivirus only inspects HTTP/HTTPS; FTP scanning requires the dedicated FortiGate FTP proxy product for the workloads described in the scenario
Apply the AV profile to the WAN interface as an 'interface-level inspection' so it covers any protocol on that link
A single antivirus profile with both HTTP and FTP scanning enabled, attached to the security policies that carry that traffic
questions.explanation: FortiGate AV profiles are multi-protocol by design: a single profile can enable scanning for HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, CIFS/SMB, and more. Tick the protocols you want and attach the same profile to any policy carrying that traffic. Two-profile setups (A) work but are unnecessary duplication. FTP scanning is fully supported (B). There is no 'interface-level' security profile (C) — security profiles attach to policies, not interfaces (interface policies exist for DoS protection, which is a separate engine).

questions.question: An administrator configures a site-to-site IPsec VPN tunnel between two FortiGates. Phase 1 completes successfully but Phase 2 never establishes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Phase 2 quick-mode selectors (source/destination subnets) do not match exactly on both peers
The pre-shared keys differ between the two sides of the tunnel in typical FortiOS deployments
The IKE proposals (encryption/auth/DH) are incompatible between the two peers
One FortiGate is in HA standby state and is blocking Phase 2 negotiation for the workloads described in the scenario
questions.explanation: Phase 1 negotiates the IKE SA; Phase 2 (quick mode) negotiates the IPsec SA and depends on the traffic selectors matching exactly on both ends. If HQ says 10.1.0.0/24 ↔ 10.2.0.0/24 but branch says 10.1.0.0/16 ↔ 10.2.0.0/16, Phase 2 cannot agree on what to encrypt and fails — even though Phase 1 was fine. A PSK mismatch (B) breaks Phase 1, not Phase 2. Incompatible Phase 1 IKE proposals (C) likewise stop Phase 1 from completing. The HA standby unit (D) doesn't terminate VPN traffic at all; the active unit handles negotiation.

questions.question: An organization wants FortiGate to block access to known botnet command-and-control servers. Which FortiGuard service provides this protection?
options: FortiGuard Anti-Spam, which quarantines messages whose bodies contain C&C URLs in typical FortiOS deployments
FortiGuard IP Reputation and Botnet C&C, which feed a live list of malicious IPs that policies can deny by source/destination
FortiGuard IPS, using exploit signatures that match C&C protocol behavior in transit for the workloads described in the scenario
FortiGuard Web Filtering, with the Malicious Websites category set to Block under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: The IP Reputation / Botnet C&C feed is the dedicated FortiGuard mechanism for this: Fortinet curates a real-time list of malicious IPs (botnet C&Cs, Tor exits, scanners, spammers) and the FortiGate policy can deny traffic to or from them. Anti-Spam (A) only acts on SMTP message bodies. IPS (C) can sometimes spot known C&C protocols but is not the primary tool for endpoint-IP-based blocking. Web Filtering (D) only catches HTTP/S traffic and misses direct IP connections on arbitrary ports.

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator needs to collect and correlate logs from multiple FortiGate devices across several branch offices into a single management console for analysis and reporting. Which Fortinet product is designed for this purpose?
options: FortiCloud, which is the cloud portal for license registration and lightweight status dashboards in typical FortiOS deployments
FortiManager, which provides centralized configuration management — not the logging and analytics platform
FortiSIEM, which correlates multi-vendor logs but is positioned as a SIEM, not the Fortinet-native log collector
FortiAnalyzer, which receives logs from FortiGates, stores them long-term, and provides pre-built reports and analytics
questions.explanation: FortiAnalyzer is Fortinet's purpose-built log collector and analytics platform: it ingests logs from many FortiGates, stores them, and provides reports, event correlation, and forensic queries. FortiCloud (A) handles registration / SaaS portals but is not the analytics platform of choice for multi-device correlation. FortiManager (B) manages configurations centrally; logs flow to FortiAnalyzer instead. FortiSIEM (C) is a broader SIEM that ingests data from many vendors — useful if you need cross-vendor correlation, but not the standard answer for centralizing FortiGate logs.

questions.question: A FortiGate security policy allows traffic from LAN to WAN but users cannot reach any websites. The FortiGate has a valid default route. Running 'diagnose debug flow' shows the traffic is accepted by the policy. What should the administrator check next?
options: Verify that NAT is enabled on the policy (or a Central SNAT entry exists) so private addresses get translated to the WAN IP
Check the FortiGuard subscription status — an expired subscription can stop forwarding altogether in typical FortiOS deployments
Verify DNS resolution by testing FQDN lookups from the client for the workloads described in the scenario
Re-import the FortiGate root CA on each client to fix HTTPS handshakes under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: The flow trace says the policy accepted the packet, so the policy match isn't the problem — the next thing to check is NAT. Without SNAT, packets leave the FortiGate carrying private (RFC1918) source addresses, and the upstream internet has no route back to them, so nothing returns. Enabling NAT on the policy (or adding a Central SNAT entry) is the fix. FortiGuard expiry (B) affects security features but does not stop traffic forwarding. DNS (C) would cause name-resolution errors, not 'no websites at all' for IPs. Re-importing CAs (D) is unrelated to basic connectivity.

questions.question: An administrator receives an alert that a FortiGate's disk is almost full due to log files. The FortiGate stores logs locally. What is the best practice for managing this in a production environment?
options: Forward logs to a FortiAnalyzer or syslog server and minimize local logging on the FortiGate
Order a larger internal storage module from Fortinet for the appliance in typical FortiOS deployments
Enable on-disk log compression and keep everything local for long-term retention
Configure aggressive local log rotation that deletes anything older than 24 hours
questions.explanation: Best practice is to offload logs to FortiAnalyzer (or a syslog/SIEM server) for retention and analysis, and keep only minimal local logging on the FortiGate. Internal disks are limited, and once full they can degrade performance or drop new logs. Replacing the disk (B) is rarely a real option on most models and doesn't scale across many sites. Compression (C) helps a little but doesn't change the underlying growth problem. Deleting after 24 hours (D) sacrifices audit and incident-response data and is not 'best practice'.

questions.question: A FortiGate is receiving IPsec VPN connections from remote FortiClients but some clients with dynamic IP addresses cannot establish the VPN. The Phase 1 is configured with the remote gateway set to a static IP. What change resolves this?
options: Change the Phase 1 remote-gateway type from 'Static IP Address' to 'Dialup User' so the FortiGate accepts inbound IKE from any source
Switch from IKEv1 to IKEv2; IKEv2 alone handles dynamic-source clients in static-peer Phase 1 configs in typical FortiOS deployments
Enable NAT-Traversal in Phase 1, which lets dynamic clients connect through any source IP for the workloads described in the scenario
Add one Phase 1 entry per possible client IP, listing each address explicitly under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: For remote-access VPNs where clients arrive from arbitrary IPs, Phase 1's remote-gateway type must be set to 'Dialup User'. That tells the FortiGate to accept incoming IKE negotiations regardless of source address (it then identifies the user by PSK + ID, certificate, or XAuth). Switching to IKEv2 (B) doesn't change the Static-vs-Dialup distinction. NAT-T (C) helps clients behind NAT but doesn't change how the gateway type accepts the connection. Listing every possible client IP (D) is impossible for genuinely dynamic addresses.

questions.question: An administrator has configured SSL VPN with FortiToken two-factor authentication (2FA). Users report that after entering their username, password, and token code, they receive an authentication failure. RADIUS logs show a successful authentication. What is the most likely cause?
options: SSL VPN does not support 2FA at all; only IPsec VPN with FortiClient does in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
FortiGate clock drift relative to the FortiToken (NTP not configured or inaccurate) — TOTP codes don't validate when the time window slips
RADIUS Accept arrived but the user's group does not map to the SSL VPN portal, so FortiGate authorizes but cannot place the user
The FortiToken Mobile license expired, so OTP validation fails silently under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
questions.explanation: The most common operational cause when RADIUS shows success but the FortiGate side fails is TOTP time drift: FortiToken codes are based on synchronized clocks, and even a couple of minutes of drift on the FortiGate (no NTP, wrong timezone, stale clock) makes every code look invalid. Ensure NTP is configured and accurate on the FortiGate. SSL VPN absolutely supports 2FA (A). Group-to-portal mapping (C) would generally produce a different symptom (portal-not-available rather than auth failure). FortiToken licenses (D) do affect new activations but expired licenses do not cause silent OTP failures on already-issued tokens in this scenario.

questions.question: A security administrator wants FortiGate to generate an alert and block traffic when it detects a port scan originating from an internal host. Which security feature should be enabled?
options: A DoS Protection policy on the internal interface using the TCP/UDP port-scan anomaly with threshold + Block action
A standard firewall policy with a custom 'all ports' service and logging on every deny in typical FortiOS deployments
A web-filter profile with the Reconnaissance category set to Block for the workloads described in the scenario
An IPS profile attached to the LAN-to-DMZ policy with only signature-based rules under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: DoS Protection policies in FortiOS include built-in anomaly detectors for TCP/UDP port scans and sweeps with configurable thresholds and actions (Pass / Block / Quarantine). Binding such a policy to the internal interface is the standard way to detect and block internal port scanners. A normal firewall policy (B) just logs denies — it doesn't recognize a scan pattern across many flows. Web filter (C) operates on URL categories, not on scan patterns. An IPS profile (D) can detect some scan signatures but is meant for known-exploit detection rather than anomaly thresholds; the DoS engine is the dedicated tool.

questions.question: A FortiGate has two virtual domains (VDOMs): VDOM_A for sales and VDOM_B for engineering. The administrator needs both VDOMs to share internet access through a single WAN link. Which configuration enables this?
options: Move the WAN interface into a special 'Global' VDOM so any VDOM can route through it directly in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Use NAT on each VDOM with a shared global address pool so traffic exits naturally toward the WAN under the standard FortiGate configuration
Configure an inter-VDOM link between VDOM_A, VDOM_B, and the VDOM containing the WAN interface, then route default traffic over the inter-VDOM link
Replicate the WAN interface into both VDOMs using ECMP routing across the copies when applied at the security-policy level in a single-VDOM topology
questions.explanation: Inter-VDOM links are virtual point-to-point interfaces internal to the FortiGate that let traffic cross VDOM boundaries. The standard 'shared internet' pattern is: one VDOM holds the WAN interface, each user VDOM has an inter-VDOM link to that VDOM, and the user VDOMs send their default route over the link. Source NAT is applied in the WAN-owning VDOM as traffic egresses. There is no 'Global' VDOM that can own shared interfaces (A) — global config exists, but interfaces still belong to a single VDOM. NAT alone (B) cannot move traffic across VDOM boundaries without an inter-VDOM link. Interfaces cannot be replicated across VDOMs (D).

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator wants to configure web filtering to allow access to the 'Video Streaming' category only for the marketing department users, while blocking it for all other users. What is the correct approach?
options: One web filter profile with Video Streaming = Allow applied to everyone, then Application Control to restrict video by user group separately in typical FortiOS deployments
URL overrides listing every video site, assigned only to the marketing LDAP group inside one shared profile for the workloads described in the scenario under the standard FortiGate configuration
Per-user web filter exceptions enabled inside the profile, with marketing users individually whitelisted when applied at the security-policy level in a single-VDOM topology
Two security policies, ordered top-down: the upper one matches the marketing FSSO/LDAP group with a permissive profile, the lower one matches everyone else with the restrictive profile
questions.explanation: Group-aware policy enforcement on FortiGate uses the policy table itself: place the permissive policy (source = marketing group, profile = allows video) above the restrictive policy (source = all, profile = blocks video). Because policies are first-match top-down, marketing matches first and everyone else falls through. Option A inverts the goal — allowing video for everyone and trying to claw it back is fragile. Maintaining URL overrides per site (B) is unsustainable. Per-user whitelisting (C) doesn't scale and is not the recommended pattern.

questions.question: A FortiGate IPS sensor has a signature with a default action of 'Pass'. The administrator changes the action to 'Block' for this specific signature. After saving, traffic matching that signature continues to pass. What should be checked?
options: Whether the FortiGuard IPS subscription is current — expired subscriptions disable manual action overrides
Whether sufficient memory is available to load the updated signature database in typical FortiOS deployments
Whether the policy applying the sensor is in NGFW mode, which ignores per-signature action changes
Whether a filter-level entry (category, severity, or OS) higher up in the sensor is forcing 'Pass' for that signature
questions.explanation: An IPS sensor evaluates filter entries (matching by category, severity, OS, target, etc.) before individual signature entries. If a filter entry above the signature override matches and is set to Pass, the filter wins — the per-signature Block never takes effect. Audit the sensor and either remove/narrow the filter entry or raise the per-signature override. The subscription (A) being expired does not silently override administrator actions. Memory (B) would surface as a different alarm. NGFW mode (C) does not invert per-signature actions inside a sensor.

questions.question: An administrator wants to ensure that only compliant endpoints (running FortiClient with current signatures) can access the internal network via SSL VPN. Which FortiGate feature enforces this requirement?
options: Configure FortiGate's own NAC profile to interrogate the endpoint every login in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Integrate FortiClient EMS with FortiGate via the Security Fabric and require an EMS compliance tag in the SSL VPN portal / policy
Use Application Control to detect the endpoint's OS and block non-compliant operating systems under the standard FortiGate configuration
Issue pre-logon certificates from FortiAuthenticator only to compliant endpoints when applied at the security-policy level
questions.explanation: FortiClient EMS evaluates endpoints (AV running, signatures current, OS patched, etc.) and assigns compliance tags. With the EMS Fabric connector in place, FortiGate can require a specific compliance tag on the SSL VPN portal or in the policy — non-compliant endpoints are denied access. NAC profiles on FortiGate (A) are used in switch/Wi-Fi NAC scenarios, not for SSL VPN compliance gating. Application Control (C) identifies traffic, not endpoint posture. Pre-logon certificates (D) provide authentication but do not check ongoing compliance state.

questions.question: FortiGate has an IPsec VPN tunnel that has been working correctly. Users report they can no longer access resources across the tunnel. What is the first CLI diagnostic command the administrator should run to verify the tunnel status?
options: get vpn ipsec tunnel summary — for a single-line view of each tunnel's Phase 1 / Phase 2 state, byte counters, and uptime
diagnose vpn ike status — for IKE SA statistics across the whole device in typical FortiOS deployments
get vpn ipsec stats tunnel — for packet/byte counters per IPsec SA for the workloads described in the scenario
diagnose debug application ike -1 — verbose IKE debugging in real time under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: `get vpn ipsec tunnel summary` gives the fastest 'is it up?' answer: one row per tunnel with Phase 1 / Phase 2 state, byte counters, and uptime. If that shows the tunnel is down, the deeper tools come next: `diagnose vpn ike status` (B) shows IKE SA stats; `get vpn ipsec stats tunnel` (C) is more verbose counter detail; `diagnose debug application ike -1` (D) is a real-time debug that you turn on after the summary has identified that something is broken, not as a first check.

questions.question: A FortiGate web filter profile is configured to redirect blocked websites to a FortiGate-hosted 'Access Denied' page. Users report the block page is not appearing — instead they see a browser connection error. What is the most likely cause?
options: SSL deep inspection is not enabled, so for HTTPS sites the FortiGate cannot terminate TLS to serve the HTML block page; the browser shows a connection-reset error instead
The block page only renders in proxy-based inspection mode and flow-based cannot deliver it in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
HTTPS administrative access must be enabled on the user-facing interface for the FortiGate to serve block pages under the standard FortiGate configuration
The FortiGuard Web Filtering license is expired and block pages are disabled until renewal when applied at the security-policy level in a single-VDOM topology
questions.explanation: To inject an HTML block page on an HTTPS request, the FortiGate must terminate the TLS session — which requires SSL deep inspection. Without it, the FortiGate simply resets the TLS handshake and the browser shows ERR_CONNECTION_RESET or a certificate error rather than the HTML page. Both proxy-based and flow-based inspection can serve block pages with SSL deep inspection in place (B). The user-facing interface's management-access settings (C) are unrelated to block-page delivery. An expired license (D) usually defaults to a permissive state, not a missing block page in this way.

questions.question: A company needs to monitor all outbound email traffic for data loss prevention (DLP). Employees send email via Microsoft 365 (SMTP over TLS on port 587). What FortiGate configuration is required to inspect this traffic?
options: Enable a DLP profile for SMTP and attach it directly; FortiGate decrypts STARTTLS transparently with no additional inspection profile
Use the Email Filter profile to intercept SMTP traffic to M365 servers before TLS is negotiated in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Create a proxy policy for SMTP only — regular policies cannot decrypt SMTP-TLS under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
Combine an SSL/SSH inspection profile that covers SMTP/STARTTLS on TCP/587 with a DLP profile, attached to the outbound policy carrying that traffic
questions.explanation: SMTP via STARTTLS on TCP/587 is encrypted end-to-end, so DLP on its own would only see ciphertext. The fix is to attach an SSL/SSH inspection profile that includes SMTPS/STARTTLS on TCP/587 (so the FortiGate decrypts and re-encrypts) plus the DLP profile on the same policy. Attaching only DLP (A) is exactly the broken state described. The Email Filter (B) covers spam/AV concerns and is not a DLP engine. Regular security policies (and not 'proxy policies' specifically) can handle SMTP DLP once an SSL inspection profile is attached, so (C) misstates the requirement.

questions.question: An administrator has configured a FortiGate policy with source address 'all' and destination address 'all' for internet access, with NAT enabled. A security audit flags this as overly permissive. Which addresses should replace 'all' for the source?
options: Replace with the RFC1918 ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) as the source set
Replace with the geographic 'Domestic' object so only same-country hosts can route out
Replace with the specific LAN-interface subnet address object (least-privilege scoping)
Replace with the inverse of the WAN address so only non-WAN sources can match
questions.explanation: Least-privilege firewall design says: scope the source to the actual LAN subnet (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24). That guarantees only legitimate internal hosts on the segment can match the internet policy. The full RFC1918 ranges (A) are too broad — they include subnets that don't exist in your environment and may be reachable via routing. A geographic 'Domestic' object (B) does not exist as a source-address concept on FortiGate (geo objects target external IPs, not internal hosts). An 'inverse of WAN' construction (D) is overly clever and still permits any internal address.

questions.question: A FortiGate is deployed at a healthcare organization. The administrator must ensure that HIPAA-regulated patient data cannot be sent via HTTP POST requests to external sites. Which FortiGate feature enforces this?
options: An IPS signature set tuned to detect HTTP POST bodies containing PHI patterns in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
An Application Control profile blocking HTTP POST to all external destinations under the standard FortiGate configuration
A Web Filter profile that blocks the Personal Storage and File Sharing categories when applied at the security-policy level
A DLP (Data Loss Prevention) sensor with regex/file-type rules matching PHI (SSN, MRN, ICD codes) applied to the outbound web policy
questions.explanation: DLP sensors are the FortiGate tool for content inspection: define patterns (regex for SSNs, file-type fingerprints for medical records, sensitive-data templates for HIPAA) and apply the sensor to the outbound HTTP/HTTPS policy with action Block + Log. IPS (A) is built around exploit signatures, not content categories, and would be brittle for HIPAA inspection. Blocking all HTTP POST (B) breaks legitimate use of nearly every modern site. Web filter (C) targets URL categories and cannot inspect message bodies for sensitive content.

questions.question: An administrator wants to implement network segmentation by creating multiple isolated networks on FortiGate. Each network segment should have its own policies and not share routing tables with others. Which FortiGate feature provides this logical separation?
options: Security zones, which group interfaces but share the host VDOM's routing table in typical FortiOS deployments
Virtual Domains (VDOMs), which give each segment its own routing table, policies, objects, and admin scope
VLAN subinterfaces, which separate at Layer 2 but share the FortiGate's routing table for the workloads described in the scenario
A 'network segmentation' profile that microsegments inside one routing instance under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: VDOMs are FortiGate's full logical-firewall partition: each VDOM has its own routing table, its own policies, its own interface assignments and admin scope. Traffic cannot cross VDOM boundaries without an explicit inter-VDOM link. Security zones (A) help group interfaces but they still share the host VDOM's routing table — they are not isolated firewall instances. VLAN subinterfaces (C) separate at L2 but share the same routing table inside the VDOM. There is no 'network segmentation profile' object as described in (D).

questions.question: An organization uses FortiGate in active-passive HA. The HA heartbeat interfaces are configured but the secondary unit shows 'out of sync' / 'unmanaged' status. What should the administrator verify?
options: That the management interfaces on both units have valid IPs in typical FortiOS deployments
That the heartbeat cable is connected to a routed Layer-3 interface, not directly between the units
That both units share the same HA group name and password and run the same FortiOS firmware version
That FortiGuard subscription serial numbers match exactly between the two units for the workloads described in the scenario
questions.explanation: HA cluster formation requires that the units agree on identity (HA group name + password) and run the same firmware build — a mismatch on either prevents the secondary from joining and produces the out-of-sync state. The management interface (A) is for out-of-band administration and is not the heartbeat path. The heartbeat is meant to run on dedicated heartbeat interfaces, directly between units (B) — moving it onto a routed L3 interface would, if anything, make things worse. FortiGuard serial numbers (D) don't have to match for HA formation.

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator needs to prevent specific hosts on the internal network from using encrypted messaging applications (Signal, Telegram) that use TLS on non-standard ports. What is the most effective approach?
options: Maintain address objects of known Signal/Telegram server IPs and deny them in the security policy
A DoS Protection policy targeting the typical ports used by messaging apps in typical FortiOS deployments
Application Control with signatures for Signal, Telegram, and the Encrypted Messaging category set to Block
SSL deep inspection on all outbound traffic plus Web Filter category blocking for the workloads described in the scenario
questions.explanation: Application Control identifies apps by their protocol fingerprint and behavior, regardless of port or CDN. Signal and Telegram are part of Fortinet's signature library and can be blocked directly under the Encrypted Messaging category or by individual app signatures. Hard-coded IP lists (A) fall apart against CDNs and dynamic infrastructure. DoS policies (B) are for flood / scan anomalies, not application gating. SSL deep inspection plus Web Filter (D) can complement Application Control but on its own targets URL categories, which is brittle for non-HTTP protocols.

questions.question: A FortiGate is sending logs but FortiAnalyzer shows no received entries. The FortiGate confirms logs are sent to the FortiAnalyzer IP. What should be checked on FortiAnalyzer?
options: That the FortiAnalyzer license includes the correct daily-GB log allowance in typical FortiOS deployments
That the FortiAnalyzer syslog daemon is enabled and listening on UDP 514 for the workloads described in the scenario
That the FortiGate is registered and authorized in FortiAnalyzer's Device Manager so its logs are accepted
That the FortiAnalyzer Fabric connector is enabled on the FortiGate to push logs under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: FortiAnalyzer requires device authorization — when a new FortiGate first contacts it, an authorization request appears in Device Manager and an administrator must approve it. Until that happens, FortiAnalyzer silently drops logs from that device. License sizing (A) affects long-term ingest rates but does not cause complete silence at zero volume. The syslog daemon (B) is mostly relevant for non-FortiGate syslog ingest; FortiGate-to-FortiAnalyzer uses OFTP, not syslog. The Fabric connector (D) is for management integration, not for log delivery.

questions.question: An administrator is configuring explicit web proxy on FortiGate for users who have their browsers set to use a proxy server. Which FortiGate configuration is needed to enable explicit proxy?
options: Enable Explicit Web Proxy on the client-facing interface (default listener TCP/8080) and create explicit-proxy policies to control access
Enable transparent proxy in the security policy so HTTP is intercepted without browser-side config in typical FortiOS deployments
An interface policy that redirects TCP/80 from clients into the proxy engine for the workloads described in the scenario
A firewall policy with service 'HTTP-PROXY' to grab browser proxy requests on TCP/8080 under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: Explicit web proxy on FortiGate is enabled by toggling 'Explicit Web Proxy' on the inward-facing interface; the FortiGate then listens on TCP/8080 by default and browsers (or a PAC/WPAD file) point at that listener. Explicit-proxy policies — separate from regular firewall policies — control who can use it and apply web filter / AV / DLP profiles. Transparent proxy (B) does the opposite — it intercepts traffic with no browser configuration and is a different feature. Interface policies (C) target DoS, not proxy redirection. A standard firewall policy with service HTTP-PROXY (D) does not enable the proxy listener itself.

questions.question: A FortiGate administrator wants to use FortiGate as a DNS server for the internal network and apply DNS filtering to block malicious domains. What configuration is required?
options: Enable DNS over HTTPS (DoH) on the WAN interface to intercept all DNS queries on TCP/443 in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Enable the DNS service on an internal interface, attach a DNS Filter profile to the DNS policy, and point clients at the FortiGate's IP for DNS resolution
Deploy FortiAuthenticator as the DNS server and let FortiGate inspect responses via IPS under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
Use an IPS sinkhole profile to redirect malicious-domain queries to a safe IP in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
questions.explanation: The native FortiGate DNS filtering pattern is: enable the DNS service on the internal interface (so FortiGate is the resolver), attach a DNS Filter profile (which uses FortiGuard's domain rating to block malicious/phishing/botnet categories), and point clients at FortiGate as their DNS server. DoH on WAN (A) would not turn FortiGate into the LAN's resolver. FortiAuthenticator (C) is an identity product, not a DNS server. IPS sinkholing (D) is a niche fallback inside the IPS engine, not the standard architecture for FortiGate-as-DNS-resolver.

questions.question: A FortiGate displays a warning: 'conserve mode'. CPU and memory usage are within normal ranges. What is the most likely cause and what action should be taken?
options: FortiGuard subscription has expired; renewing it returns the device to normal mode in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Disk usage has exceeded 90%; freeing log space releases conserve mode under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level

Free memory has dropped below a threshold (even if overall usage looks fine), so FortiGate is dropping new sessions to protect existing ones — investigate large session tables, content buffers, or memory leaks
NP7 utilization is above its hardware threshold; reducing the session table fixes it in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
questions.explanation: Conserve mode is triggered when free memory falls below a critical threshold (the GUI memory-usage gauge can still look 'normal' if you're looking at cumulative percentages). FortiGate then drops new sessions and disables some memory-hungry features to protect existing flows from a crash. The fix is to find what's consuming memory — bloated session tables, content inspection buffers, FSSO sessions — using `diagnose hardware sysinfo memory` and `diagnose sys top`. Subscription expiry (A) and disk usage (B) don't trigger conserve mode. NP7 (D) handles forwarding offload, not RAM pressure.

questions.question: An administrator must configure FortiGate to protect a web application from OWASP Top 10 attacks including SQL injection, XSS, and CSRF. Which FortiGate security profile provides web application-level protection?
options: Application Control with the Web Application category in monitor mode in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
IPS with selected web-attack signatures (SQLi, XSS, CSRF) enabled under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
Web Application Firewall (WAF) profile with SQLi / XSS / CSRF signature sets configured and attached to the inbound policy protecting the web server
Web Filter with the Malicious Websites and Phishing categories set to Block in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
questions.explanation: FortiGate's WAF profile is the right tool for OWASP Top 10 coverage: it contains signature sets specifically for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, CSRF, command injection, path traversal, etc., and attaches to the inbound security policy in front of the web server. Application Control (A) identifies apps, it isn't an injection-attack filter. IPS (B) can catch some web attacks but doesn't have the OWASP-focused signature depth of WAF. Web Filter (D) targets URL categories, not request-body injection patterns.

questions.question: An administrator needs to verify that a specific user (jsmith@company.com) was authenticated via FSSO and identify which FortiGate security policy is being applied to their traffic. Which CLI command provides this information?
options: diagnose debug authentication — enables real-time auth event logging globally in typical FortiOS deployments
get user fsso list — shows FSSO server connectivity, not per-session policy mapping for the workloads described in the scenario
show user authenticated jsmith@company.com — for per-user auth state under the standard FortiGate configuration
diagnose firewall auth list — shows all currently authenticated firewall users with IP, groups, and authentication method
questions.explanation: `diagnose firewall auth list` is the working command: it prints every authenticated firewall user along with the IP they're seen on, the groups they belong to (which is what governs policy matching), and how they authenticated (FSSO, LDAP, RADIUS, local). That's exactly what you need to verify FSSO auth and map traffic to policies. `diagnose debug authentication` (A) is not the standard command for this lookup. `get user fsso list` (B) lists FSSO server connectivity, not per-user policy data. `show user authenticated <user>` (C) is not a valid FortiOS CLI.

questions.question: A FortiGate is deployed as a perimeter firewall with multiple security profiles applied to policies. An administrator notices CPU usage is consistently above 90%. All FortiGate hardware accelerators (NP7) are enabled. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: HA heartbeat traffic is overwhelming the CPU in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
FortiGuard rating-server lookups are flooding the CPU under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
Heavyweight security profiles (proxy-based inspection, full-file AV, SSL deep inspection) cannot be offloaded to NP7/CP9 and are processed in software on the main CPU
The NP7 is handling too many concurrent sessions and needs the session table reduced in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
questions.explanation: NP7 offloads basic L3/L4 forwarding (and some flow-based inspection), and CP9 accelerates content cryptography. Proxy-based inspection, full-file AV scanning, and SSL deep inspection on high-volume policies cannot be fully offloaded and end up running on the main CPU — the typical cause of sustained high CPU on otherwise healthy NP-equipped boxes. Moving suitable policies to flow-based inspection or trimming AV/DPI profiles relieves the pressure. HA heartbeat (A) is tiny. FortiGuard rating queries (B) are lightweight. Reducing the session table (D) doesn't fix software-path inspection load.

questions.question: A FortiGate security policy has 'Log All Sessions' enabled. The administrator notices the log storage fills up quickly. They only need to log denied traffic and allowed traffic to specific sensitive servers. What is the best configuration change?
options: Switch the policy to log Security Events only (UTM events, not every session start/end), and create a separate dedicated policy for the sensitive servers with full session logging
Enable log compression to fit more entries on the same disk in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Reduce the local log retention period from 90 to 7 days under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
Disable all logging on the FortiGate and rely on SNMP traps for visibility in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
questions.explanation: 'Log All Sessions' produces a log entry per session start and end — the single biggest contributor to log volume. Switching to 'Security Events' on the general policy keeps the alerts (IPS, web filter blocks, AV hits, denies) and drops the chatter, while a narrowly-scoped policy for the sensitive servers keeps full session logging where you actually want it. Compression (B) helps a little but doesn't change generation rate. Shorter retention (C) doesn't slow incoming logs. Replacing logging with SNMP traps (D) creates a huge audit gap.

questions.question: A company's FortiGate uses OSPF to exchange routing information with an internal router. After a configuration change, the FortiGate and the router are no longer exchanging OSPF routes. Both devices are in the same area. What is the most likely cause?
options: The OSPF process IDs are different on the FortiGate and the router, preventing adjacency in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
OSPF requires a FortiGuard routing license that has not been activated under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
Both devices share the same router ID, which by itself silently breaks the adjacency in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
There is an OSPF parameter mismatch (network type, hello/dead intervals, authentication, or area type) preventing Hello packets from agreeing
questions.explanation: OSPF adjacency demands matched values across both ends for area ID, hello interval, dead interval, authentication, and network type (point-to-point vs. broadcast vs. NBMA). A single mismatch keeps the neighbors stuck at INIT or 2WAY. OSPF process IDs (A) are locally significant — they do not need to match between peers. There is no separate FortiGuard routing license (B). A duplicate router ID (C) is a real problem but typically produces a logged conflict, not a silent failure of Hello processing.

questions.question: An administrator needs to allow a specific external IP address (198.51.100.25) to manage the FortiGate via HTTPS and SSH only — no other management protocols should be accessible from that IP. What is the most precise configuration?
options: Enable HTTPS and SSH on the WAN interface and use an interface-level ACL field to restrict source IPs
Set the admin account's trusted hosts to 198.51.100.25/32 and enable only HTTPS and SSH on the WAN interface
Create an inbound WAN-to-FortiGate firewall policy permitting source 198.51.100.25 on TCP/443 and TCP/22
Place the WAN in a 'mgmt' security zone with an inferred allow-from-25 rule in typical FortiOS deployments
questions.explanation: Trusted hosts on the admin account scope which source IPs may log in as that admin, regardless of which interface they hit — set them to 198.51.100.25/32 and only HTTPS/SSH on the WAN, and you have precise per-admin source-IP control. FortiGate interfaces don't have a stand-alone source-IP ACL field (A). Forward-direction firewall policies (C) don't govern traffic destined to the FortiGate itself; that's done by per-interface administrative access and local-in policies. Security zones (D) don't have built-in admin source filtering.

questions.question: A FortiGate is forwarding logs to a FortiAnalyzer. The organization requires that FortiGate logs be retained for 1 year for compliance. FortiAnalyzer's default retention is 30 days. What must be configured on FortiAnalyzer?
options: Purchase additional FortiAnalyzer storage; extended retention then activates automatically in typical FortiOS deployments
Increase the analytics-tier retention to 365 days for everything for the workloads described in the scenario under the standard FortiGate configuration
Update the FortiAnalyzer data policy so that the archive tier retains logs for 365 days (analytics tier remains short for fast queries)
Forward all logs to a secondary FortiAnalyzer; combined retention becomes 365 days when applied at the security-policy level
questions.explanation: FortiAnalyzer separates logs into an analytics tier (fast, indexed, short-retention) and an archive tier (compressed, long-retention). Setting the archive policy to 365 days keeps logs available for compliance without bloating the fast tier. Buying more storage (A) gives you space but doesn't by itself set the retention policy. Increasing analytics retention to 365 days (B) works but burns far more disk than necessary. Forwarding to a second unit (D) replicates logs but doesn't define a retention policy on either side.

questions.question: A FortiGate receives traffic from users on VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24) and VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) via a trunk port connected to a managed switch. Users on VLAN 10 can access the internet but VLAN 20 users cannot. What should the administrator verify?
options: VLAN 20 is tagged on the switch trunk to FortiGate AND a VLAN 20 subinterface exists on the FortiGate with the correct IP
The trunk's speed/duplex matches between FortiGate and switch in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
OSPF is configured so VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 are in the same area under the standard FortiGate configuration
Spanning Tree is enabled on FortiGate so both VLANs converge when applied at the security-policy level
questions.explanation: Two things must be true together for VLAN 20 to be visible to the FortiGate: the switch must tag VLAN 20 on the trunk port leading to the FortiGate, and the FortiGate must have a VLAN 20 subinterface configured under the trunk-facing physical interface with an IP and security policy. If either is missing, VLAN 20 frames never get processed. Speed/duplex (B) would affect both VLANs equally. OSPF (C) is irrelevant to local segment connectivity. FortiGate does not run STP in this role (D).

questions.question: An administrator configures email alerts on FortiGate for critical security events. After configuration, no emails are being received despite security events occurring. What should be verified first?
options: That recipient addresses are in an approved senders list to avoid being dropped in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
That FortiGate can reach the SMTP relay: correct server IP / port (25 or 587), routing, and any policy permitting FortiGate-originated traffic to it
That the alert trigger is set to 'critical' rather than 'all' under the standard FortiGate configuration when applied at the security-policy level
That the FortiGate has a valid FortiCare contract, which is required to send email alerts in a single-VDOM topology as documented in the Fortinet administration guide
questions.explanation: The most common reason email alerts don't deliver is that FortiGate can't reach the SMTP server: wrong host or port, missing default route, or a local-in / firewall policy that blocks FortiGate-originated traffic. Use `diagnose log test` to send a probe and confirm. 'Approved senders' lists (A) operate on the receiving mail server, not FortiGate. The trigger level (C) shouldn't matter if the events are actually occurring at critical severity. There is no FortiCare-contract gating on email alerts (D).

questions.question: A FortiGate processes a session through several internal stages. The session table tracks each active flow's state. Which TWO statements about FortiGate session table entries are correct?
options: Each session entry stores the 5-tuple (source IP/port, destination IP/port, protocol) along with state, interfaces, NAT translation, and matched policy ID
Sessions have a per-VDOM TTL governed by the matched policy or the global session-ttl, and idle sessions are purged when that TTL expires
Session table entries are stored in EEPROM and survive a full power cycle without needing to be rebuilt in typical FortiOS deployments for the workloads described in the scenario
Each entry retains the full payload of the first packet, allowing later forensic recovery of session contents under the standard FortiGate configuration
questions.explanation: Correct (A): the session table really is keyed on the 5-tuple plus extra state — interfaces in/out, NAT translation, matched policy ID, and protocol state. Correct (B): sessions don't live forever; each has a TTL (defaulting to the global session-ttl, optionally overridden per policy or per service), and idle sessions are aged out. Incorrect (C): the session table is RAM-resident and must be rebuilt on reboot — only HA session sync preserves it across a failover, never across a full power cycle. Incorrect (D): the session table does not retain payload — only flow metadata. Payload capture is what `diagnose sniffer packet` is for.
